findings.quote: In Claude Code, `/code-review` hands the diff to a fresh **subagent**: a helper agent that never saw your conversation. Pass a PR number, as in `/code-review 14`, to review that PR.
findings.problem: This only holds while no skill named code-review is installed. Claude Code's docs say a project or personal `code-review` skill replaces the bundled `/code-review`; only its alias `/review` always reaches the built-in. Matt Pocock's Skills include `code-review`, and this site has readers install them with `npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills` in the practice project. For those readers, `/code-review 14` runs Matt's two-part review instead: one part checks the repo's coding standards, the other checks the Spec. It treats its argument as a git starting point (`git rev-parse 14` fails, so it asks for one) and doesn't hunt bugs. That is not the fresh bug-hunting PR review described here. The site's own code-review lesson warns about exactly this clash and sends readers to `/review` for the built-in.
findings.fix: Use the alias that always runs the built-in: "In Claude Code, `/review 14` hands PR #14's diff to a fresh **subagent**: a helper agent that never saw your conversation. (`/review` is the built-in `/code-review` under another name. Once you install Matt Pocock's Skills, his own [code-review](/learn/code-review) Skill can take the `/code-review` name.)" Optionally write `/review` in quick-7 and cpr-who-reviews as well. Their answers stay right either way, because Matt's Skill also starts its sub-agents with a fresh context.

findings.quote: If they differ, the branch has a commit the PR lacks. Put it on a fresh branch with its own PR first.
findings.problem: Different IDs don't prove the local branch holds extra work. Your copy can simply be behind the PR: a commit was added on GitHub (the Update branch button, an accepted suggestion) or pushed by an agent from another session or machine. In that case `-D` loses nothing, and this advice sends the reader to open a new PR from a stale, already-squashed branch. That PR lists the merged commits again, which is the trap the lesson itself warns about at line 380. The source lesson hedged this point; the draft dropped the hedge.
findings.fix: Replace with: "If they differ, don't delete it yet: find out what differs. Ask your agent which commits on `12-search-capitals` aren't in PR #14 (`gh pr view 14 --json commits` lists the PR's). A commit the PR lacks goes on a fresh branch with its own PR. If there's none, your copy was only behind the PR, and `-D` is safe."

Have Claude show what differs. A commit the pull request lacks goes on a fresh branch... No such commit? findings.quote: With `gh`, run `gh pr merge 14 --auto --squash`. It prints that the PR "will be automatically merged via squash when all requirements are met".
findings.problem: gh turns on auto-merge only when the PR can't merge yet. If GitHub reports the PR as mergeable now (merge state CLEAN, HAS_HOOKS or UNSTABLE), gh drops auto-merge and merges at once, printing "Squashed and merged". UNSTABLE covers checks that are running or failed but aren't required. So the agent prompt at lines 253-255 does not wait for the check: "If you want the agent to merge later, once a check finishes... Turn on auto-merge with squash for PR #14." In any repo where that check isn't required, it merges before the check finishes. That is a beginner's repo at this point in the course, since required checks come later, in Gates and How teams protect main.
findings.fix: After the gh command, add: "If nothing the repo requires is still pending, `gh` doesn't wait: `--auto` merges the PR straight away, even while checks the repo doesn't require are still running." At line 253, add: "This waits only for checks the repo requires. If the check you're waiting on isn't required, wait for it yourself, then merge."

findings.quote: The merge itself went through: only the clean-up stopped, and recent versions of `gh` print the commands to finish.
findings.problem: This mixes old and new gh behaviour. Since gh 2.99.0 ("safely handle --delete-branch with linked worktrees", #14007), gh skips only the local delete and still deletes the branch on GitHub. When the branch is open in another worktree that's clean, gh removes that worktree and deletes the branch itself. It prints the "To finish cleanup" commands only when it skips. If the other worktree is dirty, or locked by a running session, it prints only the reason. Before 2.99, gh stopped the whole clean-up with Git's error and printed no commands. A reader told "only the clean-up stopped" may go looking for a GitHub branch that's already gone.
findings.fix: "The merge itself went through. Recent versions of `gh` (2.99 and later) still delete the branch on GitHub, skip only your computer's copy, and say why, usually with the commands to finish. Older versions stop the whole clean-up with Git's error."

result.summary:
I checked every Git, GitHub and gh claim against the pinned snapshot, current GitHub Docs and the gh v2.103.3 source. Most of the lesson holds up: the merge-method table, the default squash message, the UI steps, the `gh pr merge` output and its `not mergeable`/`--admin` text, the `gh pr merge --delete-branch` behaviour, the plan and visibility rules for auto-merge and protected branches, the `gh repo edit` flags, the `subIssuesSummary` field and the `git branch -vv` `gone` output. All 10 quick checks and 10 final-test questions have exactly one clearly right answer, and each one can be answered from the lesson's own text. There are no private leftovers, and every /learn link points at the lesson that covers that thing. The Try-it dependencies exist: checking-a-pr leaves the PR ready for review, issues-and-keeping-track sets up yoga-studio with Ticket #3, and what-ci-cd-is adds the `test` check on pull requests. The validator prints ok.

Flagged claim: the old link from \"Spec\" to /learn/one-change-start-to-finish is gone. The lesson no longer mentions a Spec, and its sub-issue text links /learn/issues-and-keeping-track. Three related flagged claims repeated here are correct:
- `Closes #13, #10` closes only #13, because GitHub's docs ask for the full keyword syntax for each Issue.
- `gh issue view` given a PR number prints \"MERGED\". gh looks up issueOrPullRequest, and the pinned run on PR #89 shows that output.
- Closing does lag a moment behind the merge: PR #89 merged at 05:44:10Z, and Issue #77 closed at 05:44:13Z.

Problems found: three medium and five low.
- Medium: when the branch and PR IDs differ, the lesson says the branch has a commit the PR lacks, but the local copy may just be behind the PR.
- Medium: `gh pr merge --auto` merges straight away when nothing required is pending, so the agent prompt that asks to merge once a check finishes doesn't work in a repo where that check isn't required.
- Medium: the auto-merge Try it never moves into the yoga-studio folder, right after a Try it run in recipes.
- Low: removing the worktree is placed after deleting the branch, but Git won't delete a branch that a worktree has checked out.
- Low: the close button reads \"Close with comment\" once a comment is typed.
- Low: the worktree item in Going deeper mixes old and new gh behaviour (gh 2.99+ still deletes the GitHub branch).
- Low: the status-check search lists only checks from the past seven days.
- Low: the Matt Pocock v1.3 changelog in the sources backs nothing in this lesson.

findings.quote: Without `--staged`, `git restore` throws the edit away.
findings.problem: In quick-2 the waffle file is already staged. `git restore <file>` without `--staged` copies the staged version back onto the file on disk. The staged version already holds the waffle edit, so nothing is thrown away and the file stays staged. The option is still wrong (waffles still goes into the commit), but the Why gives a false reason. It also contradicts the lesson's own table (line 31), which says `git restore` puts the file back to "its last staged or committed version".
findings.fix: Why: `--staged` only takes the file off the list for the next commit, and the waffle edit stays on disk. Without `--staged`, `git restore` only resets the file on disk to its staged copy, so waffles stays on the list and goes into this commit. The last two act on commits, not on what's staged.
findings.evidence: Tested on git 2.43: staged recipes/waffles.md ("waffles v2"), then ran `git restore recipes/waffles.md`. The file still read "waffles v2", and `git status --short` still showed `M  recipes/waffles.md` (staged). git-restore docs: with no `--staged`, the working tree is restored from the index. /home/user/idea-to-shipped/content/github-basics/undo-and-conflicts.md:31 and :76

findings.quote: Merge `main` into the branch; don't rebase. Before you commit, show me each conflict: both sides, what you propose, and why. Wait for my OK. Then run `git diff --check` and the tests, commit and push.
findings.problem: Two gaps in the prompt the reader copies. (1) `git diff --check` only compares unstaged changes with the staging area. Once the agent has run `git add` on the resolved file, which agents often do to mark it resolved, the check prints nothing even with a marker left. The source prompt said "before staging", and the lesson's own steps 5 and 6 and quick-10 put it before `git add`. (2) "Merge `main`" can mean the local `main`, which is often behind GitHub's. Then the merge brings in nothing new, the agent pushes, and the pull request still conflicts. The lesson's terminal steps fetch and merge `origin/main`.
findings.fix: > This pull request has merge conflicts. Fetch, then merge the latest `main` from GitHub (`origin/main`) into the branch; don't rebase. Before you commit, show me each conflict: both sides, what you propose, and why. Wait for my OK. Then, before you stage anything, run `git diff --check` (it must print nothing) and the tests. Then commit and push.
findings.evidence: Tested on git 2.43 with a leftover `=======` line: `git diff --check` before `git add` printed `pancakes.md:2: leftover conflict marker` (exit 2); after `git add` it printed nothing (exit 0). Source prompt: /home/user/learn-matt-flow/lessons/0009-undo-and-conflicts.html, Tell your agent ("run git diff --check before staging (it must print nothing)"). /home/user/idea-to-shipped/content/github-basics/undo-and-conflicts.md:275, :278-279, :288, :320. /home/user/idea-to-shipped/content/github-basics/working-with-an-agent-on-github.md:142 ("Merge the latest `main`")

findings.quote: A: `git show --remerge-diff` for what it kept and dropped, `git diff --check` for leftover markers, and the tests.
findings.problem: The card asks what you check after an agent has resolved a conflict. In this lesson's flow, the agent has already committed and pushed by then. After the commit, `git diff --check` compares the folder with the staging area, and both match the commit. So it prints nothing even when the committed file still holds a marker. The reader gets a false all-clear.
findings.fix: A: `git show --remerge-diff` for what it kept and dropped (a marker it left shows up as a plain line), `git diff --check HEAD~1` for markers left in the merge, and the tests. Alternatively, keep plain `git diff --check`, but as something the agent runs before it stages, as in step 5.
findings.evidence: Tested on git 2.43: after `git commit --no-edit` with a marker left in pancakes.md, `git diff --check` printed nothing (exit 0). `git diff --check HEAD^1` and `git show --check --first-parent` both printed `pancakes.md:2: leftover conflict marker`. `HEAD~1` is the same commit as `HEAD^1`. /home/user/idea-to-shipped/content/github-basics/undo-and-conflicts.md:433-434

findings.quote: Nothing is committed yet. Which undo fits?
findings.problem: Read literally, "Nothing is committed yet" means a repo with no commits. That's the classic moment an agent's first `git add .` stages `.env`. There, the "right" answer fails: `git restore --staged .env` stops with `fatal: could not resolve HEAD`, and git's own hint is `git rm --cached <file>`. The three other options fail too, so no option works under the literal reading.
findings.fix: Reword the prompt to "The repo has earlier commits, but this change isn't committed yet." Change the Why's ending to "and `.env` isn't in any commit yet." Optionally add after line 68: "Before a repo's first commit, git's hint is `git rm --cached <file>` instead, because there's no commit to restore from."
findings.evidence: Tested on git 2.43: `git init`, then `git add .env`. `git status` showed `(use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)`, and `git restore --staged .env` failed with `fatal: could not resolve HEAD` (exit 128). The bug is still open in git's tracker: https://git.issues.gerritcodereview.com/issues/40000076 ("git restore --staged errors when HEAD is unborn"). /home/user/idea-to-shipped/content/github-basics/undo-and-conflicts.md:42, :47

findings.quote: - [ ] One you pushed an hour ago to a branch that nobody else has opened.
findings.problem: This wrong option isn't clearly wrong for a careful reader. The rule the lesson quotes just above (line 115) forbids rewriting commits that "exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on". Both conditions must hold, and nobody has built on this branch. The course's Push, pull and remotes lesson also teaches rebasing your own pushed branch and pushing with `git push --force-with-lease`. So a reader can defend this option as safe, which leaves two arguable answers.
findings.fix: Make the option clearly shared, e.g. "- [ ] One you pushed an hour ago, which a teammate has since pulled and built on." Change the Why to "A commit a teammate has pulled is shared". If the course wants the stricter rule (never rewrite once pushed), quote Pro Git's amend rule at line 115 instead: "Only amend commits that are still local and have not been pushed somewhere." Then reconcile the `--force-with-lease` passage in push-pull-and-remotes.
findings.evidence: /home/user/idea-to-shipped/content/github-basics/undo-and-conflicts.md:115, :122, :125. /home/user/idea-to-shipped/content/github-basics/push-pull-and-remotes.md:225-227 (rebase, then `git push --force-with-lease`). https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Undoing-Things ("Only amend commits that are still local and have not been pushed somewhere.")

findings.quote: Different lines merge on their own, though you still run the tests.
findings.problem: Changes on lines right next to each other conflict even though they're different lines: git treats touching changes as one spot. In a short recipe file, one pull request changing "Serves 4." and another changing the next line, "Ready in 20 minutes.", is exactly that case. The Why's "Git stops only where…" and "Different lines merge on their own" teach a rule that real merges break. GitHub itself only says changes on different lines "usually" merge without help.
findings.fix: Why: Git stops where it can't safely pick a side: the same lines changed differently, or a deleted file that the other side edited. Changes a few lines apart merge on their own, though changes on lines right next to each other can still conflict. Either way, run the tests.
